classical_baseline: The paper compares against classical Monte Carlo simulation and, for SDEs, classical multilevel Monte Carlo. It also mentions direct sampling in the analytically solvable Black-Scholes case and binomial option pricing as a classical alternative model.
classical_baseline_quotes: Monte Carlo (MC) methods are basic tools with a provable complexity analysis.

To reduce such an expensive computational cost, multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) methods have attracted very considerable attention recently, and have successfully been applied to simulate SDEs with applications in ﬁnance [28, 29].
Classically, to apply MLMC, a numerical scheme of strong order r > 1 is usually suﬃcient to obtain a complexity of eO(1/ϵ2).
The binomial option pricing model, a.k.a. the binomial lattice model, provides a discrete time (lattice-based) approximation to the Black–Scholes model [19, 37, 56].
classical_difficulty: The paper says classical Monte Carlo is expensive because each sample may require simulating an SDE path many times, and for general SDEs the cost scales poorly with precision. It states that with a strong order 1 scheme the total cost is O(1/ϵ3), and more generally classical Monte Carlo is O(ϵ−2−1/r); it also notes that higher-order schemes are hard to implement and require stronger smoothness assumptions.
classical_difficulty_quotes: It is often computationally expensive to estimate E[Y ], since a scheme that approximates the SDE is necessarily run many times to average over the randomness.

However, a challenge faced by Monte Carlo occurs when creating each sample is costly, so even quadratic dependence on ϵ may result in an computational complexity signiﬁcantly larger than O(1/ϵ2) in practice.
Under this circumstance, the computational complexity of classical Monte Carlo simulation is O(1/ϵ3) in total.

Usually, it is challenging to perform a scheme with large r, due to the higher smoothness requirement of the SDE, and, in practice, it is harder to implement explicit forms of higher strong order schemes [11, 42, 43]. So the acceleration is moderate in practice.
business_stakes: The paper explicitly says the problem matters for option and derivative pricing, and that Greeks are essential for hedging portfolios. It also notes that lower risk is preferable in financial products and that correctly identifying sensitivity is crucial to hedging.
business_stakes_quotes: Computing these is essential to hedge portfolios, and therefore it is even more important than pricing the option itself.

If two ﬁnancial products have similar expected return, the one with lower risk is usually preferable because people would like to ensure a positive rate of return earnings under most situations and are not willing to take a risk.
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit and finance-focused; classical difficulty is stated in complexity terms and in implementation/smoothness constraints.
